meta.titre: Introducing a noun clause with 'that' after verbs and adjectives of certainty

sections.contenu_markdown: After 'certain', 'sure', 'say', or 'think', English almost always slips in a small but essential word: 'that'.

'That' introduces a noun clause functioning as the object of a verb or complement of an adjective expressing certainty, belief, or statement. To combine two sentences, the second sentence becomes the 'that'-clause following the first.

sections.enonce_markdown: Combine: 'Mbarga is quite certain. He will be there.' (that)
sections.conclusion_markdown: Mbarga is quite certain that he will be there.

items.erreur_markdown: Omitting 'that' when the exercise explicitly requires using it.
items.pourquoi_faux: Although 'that' can be dropped informally in everyday English, this sentence-combining exercise specifically requires its use.
items.correction_markdown: Always use the word given in brackets explicitly when the exercise instructs you to link sentences with it.

items.enonce_markdown: Combine using 'that': 'I think. It will rain today.'
items.solution_markdown: I think that it will rain today.

items_markdown: 'That' introduces a noun clause after verbs/adjectives of certainty or statement
Use it explicitly when the exercise requires it
